title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: who is named, who is hidden, how much is left

questions.prompt: Turn this sentence round so that it begins with the guide. Nothing tells you which tense to use except the sentence itself: "In 2019, a group of law students wrote the first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax."

options.text: The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax is written by a group of law students in 2019.
The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax was wrote by a group of law students in 2019.
The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax has been written by a group of law students in 2019.
The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax was written by a group of law students in 2019.

questions.explanation: "The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax was written by a group of law students in 2019." is right: the object becomes the subject, the verb becomes be plus the past participle, and be copies the tense of the active verb, which was the past simple wrote, so it becomes was. The date 2019 confirms it and leaves no second tense defensible. "The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax is written by a group of law students in 2019." puts a present next to a finished date, which no English sentence does. "The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax was wrote by a group of law students in 2019." keeps the past simple where the participle is needed: after be it is always written. And "The first guide to tenants' rights in Sfax has been written by a group of law students in 2019." is a well built passive of the present perfect, but a perfect tense never accepts a finished date, so the sentence breaks on in 2019.

questions.prompt: A plaque in a school corridor reads: "This library was given to the school in 1997 and has been open every school day since." A pupil asks who gave the library. What is the honest answer?

options.text: The school gave it.
It was given by the pupils.
Nobody gave it.
The plaque does not say.

questions.explanation: "The plaque does not say." is the honest answer: the doer of a passive sentence appears only after by, and this sentence has no by phrase at all, so the giver has been left out on purpose. "The school gave it." confuses the two nouns the sentence does name: the library is the subject, the thing that was given, and the school is what received it; neither of them gave anything. "It was given by the pupils." invents an agent, and inventing one is exactly what a reader may never do. And "Nobody gave it." turns a silence into a denial: the plaque does not say that no one gave the library, it simply does not say who did.

questions.prompt: An association in El Kef prints this note: "Every family that applies before 30 April is visited by a volunteer. A place in the summer school is offered to the children of the families that are visited, as long as places remain." Emna's family applied on 12 April and was visited last week. What can you conclude?

options.text: The children of her family are certain to get a place.
Her family applied too late to be visited.
A place may still be offered to them.
A volunteer was visited by her family.

questions.explanation: "A place may still be offered to them." is exactly what the note allows: her family applied inside the deadline and has been visited, so it has passed both conditions, but the last four words, as long as places remain, keep the offer open rather than promise it. "The children of her family are certain to get a place." reads those four words away and turns a condition into a guarantee. "Her family applied too late to be visited." is contradicted twice over, by the date 12 April and by the visit that has already happened. And "A volunteer was visited by her family." reverses the passive of the first line: there the family is the subject that receives the visit and the volunteer is the agent who makes it, so this option swaps the two.

questions.prompt: A speaker at a meeting in Sousse says: "The centre has helped ___ to start a business, far more than it ever hoped, and it has done it with ___, because almost everything is lent by the families themselves." Which pair completes the sentence?

options.text: a little women / a lot of money
a lot of women / a little money
a few women / a lot of money
a lot of women / a few money

questions.explanation: "a lot of women / a little money" fits both gaps and both meanings: women can be counted and the speaker says far more than it ever hoped, so the first gap needs the quantifier of a large quantity, a lot of, which takes countable nouns as easily as uncountable ones; money cannot be counted and the last clause explains that the families lend almost everything, so the centre spends only a small amount, which is a little. "a little women / a lot of money" gets both nouns the wrong way round: a little never stands in front of a countable plural. "a few women / a lot of money" is well built but says the opposite of the sentence twice: a few means not many, against far more than it ever hoped, and a lot of money is contradicted by the families who lend almost everything. And "a lot of women / a few money" is right in the first gap and impossible in the second, since a few asks for a noun you can count and money is not one.

questions.prompt: A newspaper line reads: "The two prizes were presented by the head of the school." Which sentence says exactly the same thing, but starts with the person instead of the prizes?

options.text: The head of the school presented the two prizes.
The head of the school was presented the two prizes.
The head of the school presents the two prizes.
The two prizes presented the head of the school.

questions.explanation: "The head of the school presented the two prizes." is right: read the three steps backwards. The agent after by becomes the subject, be disappears, and the participle presented goes back to being a past simple, which keeps the tense that were carried. "The head of the school was presented the two prizes." is still a passive, and it makes the head the person who receives, so it says the opposite of the original. "The head of the school presents the two prizes." moves the event into the present, although were is a past; the voice may change, the tense may not. And "The two prizes presented the head of the school." simply swaps the two nouns and leaves the prizes doing the presenting.

questions.prompt: A museum in Kairouan is printing the card for one of its display cases. The curator hesitates between two lines. Line 1: "This carpet was woven in 1890." Line 2: "This carpet was woven in 1890 by the women of a single family." The museum wants each card to teach the visitor something they could not have guessed. Which line goes on the card, and for what reason?

options.text: Line 2, because the agent is what the visitor cannot guess.
Line 1, because a passive sentence never names its agent.
Line 2, because every passive sentence needs a by phrase.
Line 1, because the agent of a passive sentence is always obvious.

questions.explanation: "Line 2, because the agent is what the visitor cannot guess." is the decision and the reason together: you keep by plus the agent when the agent is news, and here it is the whole point of the card, since nobody looking at a carpet could work out that one family's women wove it. "Line 1, because a passive sentence never names its agent." states a rule that does not exist: a passive may name its agent whenever the agent is worth naming. "Line 2, because every passive sentence needs a by phrase." reaches the right line by the wrong road, and the road matters, because that rule would also force you to write by somebody after a stolen bag. And "Line 1, because the agent of a passive sentence is always obvious." is the reason for dropping an agent, not for dropping this one: the weavers of an 1890 carpet are the opposite of obvious.
